title: Classification of vegetable crops
competency: Classify vegetable crops by edible part, temperature requirement and life cycle.

keywords.def: A vegetable whose root is eaten: carrot, radish, cassava, sweet potato, beet.
A vegetable whose bulb (a short stem with swollen fleshy leaf bases) is eaten: onion, garlic.
A vegetable grown for its leaves or stems: cabbage, Swiss chard, celery, lettuce, asparagus.
A vegetable whose flowers are eaten: cauliflower, broccoli.
A vegetable whose fruit is eaten, either immature (cucumber, eggplant) or mature (tomato, pumpkin).
A tropical or sub-tropical vegetable adapted to 18–29 °C that cannot tolerate frost.
A temperate vegetable that grows well in cooler regions and needs cool weather to flower and seed.
Able to tolerate frost without injury (some cool-season crops).
Unable to tolerate frost (warm-season crops; very tender ones are the most sensitive).
A crop that completes its life cycle in a single year.
A crop that needs two growing seasons: vegetative parts in the first, reproductive parts in the second.
A crop that grows for more than two growing seasons; may produce for up to ten years.

en.text: Vegetables can be grouped by the part we eat. The book names root vegetables (carrot, radish, cassava, sweet potato, beet), leafy vegetables grown for leaves or stems (cabbage, Swiss chard, celery, lettuce, asparagus) and flower vegetables (cauliflower, broccoli). Garlic, listed by the book as a root, is really a bulb like onion. Other groups are tubers (potato, a swollen stem), immature fruits (cucumber, eggplant), mature fruits (tomato, pumpkin) and seeds or pods (peas, green beans).

en.text: Warm-season (tropical and sub-tropical) vegetables are adapted to 18–29 °C, grow well only in warm areas and cannot tolerate frost, so they are called tender: cucumber, eggplant, pepper, snap bean, sweet potato, tomato, watermelon. Cool-season (temperate) vegetables grow well in cooler regions and need cool weather to flower and seed: broccoli, celery, cabbage, garlic, kale, onion, pea, radish, spinach. They are often small, shallow rooted and respond more to nitrogen. Hardy ones tolerate frost; semi-hardy ones only light frost.

en.text: By life cycle, annuals such as spinach, lettuce and beans complete their life in a single year; most vegetables are annuals. Biennials such as carrot, cabbage and beet need two growing seasons: vegetative parts in the first and reproductive parts in the second, and many need cold to flower. Perennials such as asparagus and artichoke grow for more than two seasons and can stay in production for up to ten years.

notes.text: p.10: garlic is listed as a root vegetable. Its edible part is a bulb (short stem with swollen leaf bases/cloves), so the lesson teaches garlic with onion as a bulb vegetable.

p.11 says all cool-season crops are "hardy" and tolerate frost without injury, but the p.12 table splits them into hardy and semi-hardy (light frost only). The p.12 table is a second "Table 1.2" (should be 1.3) and lacks a comma in "pea radish".
Added: bulb, tuber, immature/mature fruit and seed/pod groups. The text defines only root, leafy and flower vegetables, but the Review Exercise uses immature- and mature-fruit vegetables.
